background.definition: Pain in the shoulder can be due to overuse, trauma, osteoarthritis, or muscle weakness that results in stress on stabilizing ligaments. It can also be referred from other structures around the shoulder.

list.listitem: Approximately 1 in 100 patients who visit their primary care physician have a chief complaint of shoulder pain.
Shoulder pain is the third most frequent musculoskeletal malady in the general population.
Shoulder issues are the second most common musculoskeletal complaint seen by primary care sports medicine physicians.
Impingement syndrome (rotator cuff tendinitis, tendinosis, subacromial bursitis, rotator cuff tears).
Instability (anterior, posterior, multidirectional because of subluxation/dislocation).
Capsulolabral pathology.
Adhesive capsulitis.
Glenohumeral joint arthritis.
Fractures (proximal humerus, scapula, clavicle).
Sternoclavicular subluxation/dislocation.
Acromioclavicular injuries (arthritis, separation).
Brachial plexopathy.
Cervical radiculopathy.
Referred pain, especially from gall bladder.

Shoulder pain can be due to inflammation or degeneration from bony changes (fracture, arthritis), musculoligamentous damage (tendinosis, tears), bursa (bursitis), or capsule and labrum (stretched and/or torn).
Two main classifications for shoulder pain are trauma and overuse injury.

Differential.Differential_Features: Lateral shoulder pain esepcially while sleeping, full passive range of motion (ROM), sometimes full active ROM, full strength
Full passive ROM, decreased active ROM, decreased strength
Markedly decreased active and passive ROM especially with external rotation and shoulder elevation, full strength, no bony changes on x-ray
Somewhat decreased active and passive ROM, full strength, bony changes on x-ray
Mechanism of overuse or trauma, full strength, positive labral physical examination and MRI arthrogram
Anterior shoulder pain, mechanism fall on the anterior shoulder
Acute or recurrent dislocations with history of laxity, and positive instability testing, and characteristic radiographic changes
Location (clavicle, humerus, scapula) and trauma mechanism

list.listitem: Obtain a history of the onset and duration of pain, recent trauma, shoulder use (sports, work activities), and whether the pain occurs at night. A simple clinical decision rule can assist in diagnosis of rotator cuff tears.

If the location of the pain is deep in the shoulder, consider impingement, adhesive capsulitis, capsulolabral pathology, arthritis, or proximal humerus fracture. If there is decreased passive ROM, consider adhesive capsulitis, arthritis, proximal humerus fracture, or loose body.
If there is decreased active ROM but full passive ROM, consider rotator cuff tears, impingement, instability, or capsulolabral pathology.

If there is decreased strength with full passive ROM, consider rotator cuff tears or pain due to acute rotator cuff tendinosis, or brachial plexopathy. If there is history of subluxation or dislocation consider instability.
If there is a chronic overuse injury (overhead athletes or laborers), consider rotator cuff tendinosis, labral pathology, or subacromial bursitis.
The overall clinical examination is very sensitive but not very specific for rotator cuff tear.
Hawkins-Kennedy, Neer, empty can (Jobe), Speed's and Yergason's tests are not very accurate. Positive results of combination of these exams increases the likelihood of the diagnosis.

For detection of biceps tendon pathology, a study in 101 patients undergoing surgery concluded that the upper cut test was most sensitive (arm flexed to 90 degrees, examiner places contralateral hand over patient's hand, and asks the patient to make an upper cut punching move against resistance, pain or pop is a positive test).
This was confirmed in a second series with 65 patients.

The most accurate single tests for diagnosing infraspinatus tendon tears in adults are the drop sign and the resisted external rotation test (RERT). The most accurate combination of tests includes the RERT and the Patte sign. No clinical tests in isolation or combination can accurately discriminate between partial thickness and full thickness tears. See below for details on how to perform each test:

The drop sign: the arm is passively elevated to 90 degrees with the examiner supporting the elbow with one hand while rotating the arm to maximal external rotation with the other hand. The patient is asked to hold this position for 10 seconds. The result is considered positive if the arm drops back to internal rotation by more than 5 degrees.

The RERT: with the arm at zero degrees of abduction, the elbow at 90 degrees of flexion, and the shoulder at a neutral rotation, the patient is asked to externally rotate the arm against the examiner's resistance, with muscle weakness (not pain alone) considered a positive result.

The Patte sign: with the arm at 90 degrees of elevation and 90 degrees of external rotation, and with the elbow at 90 degrees of flexion, the patients is asked to externally rotate the arm against the examiner's resistance. Either pain or weakness is considered a positive test result.

The clunk, anterior release, and relocation tests are accurate for instability or torn labrum. Apprehension tests (external rotation while supine—test is positive if patient feels unstable or has pain) and relocation tests (anterior force repositioning shoulder back into stable position) are 70% to 80% sensitive and 90% to 95% specific for anterior instability.Several tests have high specificity but relatively low sensitivity (ranging from 21% to 70%) for superior labrum A-P (SLAP) lesions.

The Neer sign (internal rotation and passive forward flexion—test positive with pain along arc) and Hawkins sign (internal rotation of the arm in 90 degrees forward flexion and 90 degrees elbow flexion—test positive with pain) are moderately sensitive and somewhat less specific for impingement.

The Gerber or "lift off" test (dorsum of hand on affected side placed behind back on the mid-lumbar spine—positive test is inability to lift hand off spine without pain) has good accuracy for impingement (LR+ 3.3, LR– 0.1).
Subscapularis tear
A systematic review of 5 studies concluded that the bear hug test (LR+ 4.3, LR- 0.4) and belly off test (LR+ 10.1, LR- 0.15) were most accurate for diagnosis of subscapularis tear.

Physical examination findings that are most accurate in diagnosing traumatic shoulder instability in an orthopedic referral setting include the release test, the relocation test, and the anterior drawer test.

A systematic review concluded that the most specific test combination for suspected AC joint pathology is the Paxinos sign and O'Brien's test performed in series where both are positive (LR+ 2.7). The combination that is best at ruling out AC pathology is when both Paxinos sign and the Hawkins-Kennedy test are normal (LR- 0.35).

Shoulder radiographs are recommended for patients with acute trauma. Patients with normal radiographs but significant symptoms should have MRI. Patients with subacute shoulder pain should have MRI or MR arthrogram; the former is preferred for patients older than 35 years.

A systematic review of 30 studies found pooled likelihood ratios of 38 and 0.24 for high resolution ultrasound for the diagnosis of biceps tendon dislocation, and similar values for complete rupture of the biceps tendon.

ACR Appropriateness Criteria for patients with acute shoulder trauma: (1) Begin for most patients with radiography, (2) ultrasound is very accurate for diagnosis of rotator cuff injury but not for deep soft tissue assessment, (3) following physical exam and radiography, most patients will require MRI or MR arthrography for definitive diagnosis of clinically suspected soft tissue injuries and CT for suspected fracture, and (4) CT angiography is appropriate for suspected vascular injury and bone scintigraphy for patients with suspected complex regional pain syndrome in the post-acute phase.
The accuracy of rotator cuff tear diagnosis is similar for MRI and ultrasound. The best initial test should be selected based on cost, local expertise, and availability.

A systematic review identified studies with low risk of bias (7 studies for ultrasound and magnetic resonance arthrography [MRA], 10 for MRI, 552 - 685 total patients). For the diagnosis of full or partial thickness rotator cuff tears, ultrasound was 76% sensitive and 90% specific (LR+ 7.6, LR- 0.3), MRI was 91% sensitive and 89% specific (LR+ 8.3, LR- 0.1), and MRA was 83% sensitive and 95% specific (LR+ 16.6, LR- 0.2). For full thickness tears, ultrasound was 87% sensitive and 94% specific (LR+ 14.5, LR- 0.1), MRI was 83% sensitive and 91% specific (LR+ 9.2, LR- 0.2), and MRA was 83% sensitive and 96% specific (LR+ 21, LR- 0.2). Accuracy was worse for partial thickness tears, for ultrasound sensitivity was only 43% and specificity 94% (LR+ 7.2, LR- 0.6), MRI was 64% sensitive and 95% specific (LR+ 13, LR- 0.4), and MRA was 81% sensitive and 97% specific (LR+ 27, LR- 0.2).

A Cochrane review found comparable diagnostic accuracy of MRI, MRA and ultrasound in diagnosing full thickness rotator cuff tears in patients being considered for surgery. While MRI and ultrasound have similar diagnostic performance in detecting any rotator cuff tear, they both have poor sensitivity in diagnosing partial thickness tears, with ultrasound appearing less sensitive than MRI.

For diagnosis of bursal-sided partial thickness rotator cuff tears, a systematic review of 12 studies with 1740 patients found that MRA was 77% sensitive and 98% specific (LR+ 39, LR- 0.13) and that MRI was 77% sensitive and 96% specific (LR+ 19, LR- 0.23).
For patients in whom MRI or CT are inconclusive, double-contrast plain arthrogram or CT arthrogram should be considered.
In a study of 80 patients with shoulder pain and clinically suspected supraspinatus lesion, ultrasound was only 36% sensitive (but 92% specific) compared with the reference standard of MRI.

Key MRI findings indicating adhesive capsulitis include coracohumeral ligament thickening (diagnostic odds ratio [DOR] 13), fat obliteration of the roator interval (DOR 8), rotator interval enhancement (DOR 44), axillary joint capsule enhancement (DOR 52), and inferior glenohumeral ligament hyperintensity (DOR 31).
A simple clinical decision rule can help identify patients at low, moderate, or high risk of rotator cuff tears.

Clinical decision rules to predict the response to physiotherapy interventions have limited clinical validity. The same is true for clinical prediction rules to identify patients who are more likely to benefit from cervicothoracic manipulation.
A general approach to diagnose shoulder pain includes visual inspection and palpation for abnormal anatomy or signs of inflammation, active and passive ROM testing, and muscle strength testing.
Also evaluate the patient for pain, limited range, and instability. The location of pain may indicate the cause (if anterior shoulder or clavicle, focus on AC joint and clavicular injuries).
MRI and ultrasound are both imaging options to evaluate further when patients have abnormalities on physical examination and don't get better with conservative treatment.
